note: Tier D is refused from every package, first-party included. v3 does not schematise Tier D parameters, and carries no vector exercising one — but the refusals themselves are required. A rule with no vector is a rule an implementation can omit and still claim conformance.
refusal_note: `error` is the class a conforming loader raises. A Tier D declaration is a validation error, not a security error, and the same one from every package: v2 raised a security error for community packages because provenance decided who held the authority. In v3 nobody holds it, so provenance is not the question. `must_name` lists identifiers the message must contain.
isolation_note: Each manifest is valid in every respect except the one the case names. A vector carrying a second defect lets a conforming implementation refuse for that instead and never reach the boundary under test, which reports coverage that does not exist.
tier_d_in_defaults_note: The contract's Vectors section asks for a package whose trigger default actions include a Tier D action. No manifest makes that the only defect: an action absent from `actions.available` is refused as an undeclared default, one declared at `D` is refused by the Tier D declaration rule, and one declared below `D` is refused by the minimum-tier rule. The three cases here cover those paths separately rather than one vector that could be refused for any of them.
action_registry_note: Minimum tiers for the actions these cases name. The real registry is runtime-owned and outside this contract; this is a fixture, so a consumer with no registry of its own — an authoring SDK, a catalogue — evaluates these cases against it and reaches the same verdict as a runtime. Physical capability is an outcome on a commissioned zone, never an actuator name: the one requestable outcome is open_protected_circuit at a hard floor, and no entry holds a Tier D floor, because D is a licence a registry entry is in no position to assert. close_protected_circuit is present at C because the runtime does perform it — under local arm and reset — so a loader refusing it merely as an unknown name has not implemented the rule; the case that refuses it is discriminated by the entry being governed.

cases.name: trigger_declaring_tier_d_refused
cases.why: Tier D fires before any LLM and cannot be overridden. It is the one tier that removes the operator rather than adding one.

cases.name: first_party_trigger_declaring_tier_d_refused
cases.why: The `bundled` sentinel does not buy Tier D. v2 accepted it from packages shipping with the runtime; that was containment, not ownership, and left the safety envelope a property of which skills are installed.

cases.name: tier_d_action_in_available_refused
cases.why: An action declared at D names a licence, not a floor. No package holds it; the protective outcome is registered at a hard floor and reaches D only through a safety condition.

cases.name: physical_request_in_tier_a_defaults_dispatches_at_its_floor
cases.why: The request's own floor governs its dispatch, not the trigger's tier: a Tier A observation may propose an isolation, and the proposal waits for approval at C. The trigger confers nothing either way. The case this replaced encoded a registry entry with a Tier D floor, which the contract now names as a category error rather than a rule to vector.
cases.note: Refused because `emergency_cutoff` has minimum tier D in `action_registry` and the package declares it at C. The fixture carries that minimum, so no consumer needs a registry of its own to run this case.

cases.name: default_action_not_declared_in_available_refused
cases.why: A v3 invariant in its own right, and the rule that makes the Tier D default-list case untestable in isolation — so it is covered deliberately here rather than incidentally there. `log_to_dashboard` is a Tier A action, so nothing about Tier D is involved.

cases.name: bypass_llm_refused_on_any_trigger
cases.why: `bypass_llm` is the Tier D execution property. A package reaching it under another tier would have Tier D behaviour without the label.

cases.name: escalation_to_tier_c_accepted
cases.why: A package may raise an action's tier to at most C. The cap is what makes the Tier D prohibition meaningful rather than cosmetic.

cases.name: close_protected_circuit_never_requestable_refused
cases.why: Restoring the load is what local arm and local reset do, under the trip-state rules, at the device. The safety-profile contract forbids it as a profile outcome; refusing it from a package keeps the path closed from the other side. The fixture governs the outcome, so a refusal here proves the never-requestable rule and not merely that the name is unknown.

cases.name: legacy_actuator_name_refused_naming_its_outcome
cases.why: trip_relay is how a v2 package says open_protected_circuit on the device's zone. A name asserts what is wired; the binding records a circuit mapping, not what the relay is attached to. The refusal names the outcome so an author knows what to write instead.

cases.name: outcome_declared_below_its_floor_refused
cases.why: Isolating a protected circuit is hard consequence on every zone; the floor is the registry's reviewed judgement and a package cannot lower it. requires_approval is set so the trigger is valid on its own terms and the floor is the only defect.

cases.name: parameterised_physical_action_accepted_at_its_floor
cases.why: coap_command is the one physical action whose target is chosen at dispatch rather than resolved on a commissioned zone. It is retained at floor B outside the outcome vocabulary; which layer governs its target is unresolved and tracked separately.

physical_vocabulary_note: A package requests a physical act as an outcome, resolved on the zone the trigger's sensor belongs to. close_protected_circuit is never requestable from a package — it is reserved to local arm and reset — and the actuator-specific legacy names are v2 vocabulary, refused in v3 naming the outcome they meant.
